Author’s comment: And this is another explanation of the verse and transmitted from some of the earliest exegetes of the Qurʾan.

(11) In Maʿānī al-Akhbār, it is narrated from Thaʿlaba b. Maymūn, from one of our companions, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh, concerning the words of God Almighty: the Knower of the sensible and the Unseen. He said: ‘The Unseen refers to what has not occurred, and the sensible to what has already taken place.’

Author’s comment: The meaning of ‘what has not occurred’ is not something that is still non-existent: A potentiality that has not yet entered the circumstances of actuality. W hat he mentioned are some examples of this, and this is obvious.

(12) In Al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī reports from Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil, all of whomreport via ʿAtāʾ b. Yasār from Ibn ʿAbbās that Arbad b. Qays and ʿĀmir b. al-Ṭufayl came to Medina to the Messenger of God. They approached him while he was sitting and sat before him. ʿĀmir asked, ‘What will you grant me if I embrace Islam?’ The Prophet replied: ‘For you is what is for the Muslims and upon you is what is upon them.’ He said, ‘Will you assign the command to me after you if I embrace Islam?’ He said, ‘Neither for you nor for your people, but you shall lead your own people.’ He said, ‘Then assign to me the pastures, and for you the cities.’ The Prophet said, ‘No.’ As they left

his presence, he said, ‘I will surely fill it against you with horses and men.’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘God will prevent you.’

W hen Arbad and ʿĀmir exited, ʿĀmir said, ‘O Arbad, I will distract Muḥammad with talk and you strike him with the sword, for if Muḥammad is killed, the people will not demand more than being content with the blood-money, and they will be averse to war, so we will give them the blood-money.’ Arbad said, ‘Do it.’ So, they returned and ʿĀmir said, ‘O Muḥammad, stand with me, I want to talk to you.’ He stood with him, and they went to the wall. ʿĀmir was talking to him and Arbad tried to draw the sword. When he put his hand on the handle of the sword to draw it, it clung to it, and he could not unsheathe it. And Arbad delayed ʿĀmir in striking, so the Messenger of God turned and saw Arbad and what he

was doing and turned away from them. ʿĀmir said to Arbad, ‘Why did you hold back?’ He said, ‘I put my hand on the handle of the sword and it became stuck.’

When ʿĀmir and Arbad left the presence of the Messenger of God and traveled until they were at Ḥarra Raqim. They set down, and Saʿd b. Muʿādh and Usayd b. Ḥuḍāyr came out to them and said, “You are uncovered, O enemies of God, may God curse you both,”

and attacked them. ʿĀmir said, “Who is this, O Saʿd?” Saʿd said, “This is Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr al-Katāʾib.” He said, “By God, surely Ḥuḍayr was a friend to me.”

When they were at Raqim, God sent a lightning bolt upon Arbad, killing him. And ʿĀmir continued on his way until when he was at al-Kharīb. There, God afflicted him with an ulcer, and death overtook him therein. God revealed the verses: Allah knows what every

female carries … He has guardian angels, to his front and his rear …. (13:8–11). He explained: “Guardian angels protect M uḥammad by God’s command, then he mentioned Arbad and his manner of death, then said: ‘It is He who shows you the lightning, inspiring fear and hope …though He is great in might’ (13:12-13).

Author’s comment: A tradition with a similar meaning is narrated from al-Ṭabarī and Abū Shaykh from Ibn Zayd; at the end of it, Labīd spoke about his brother Arbad while mourning him:

‘I fear for Arbad the thunderbolts and I do not, Fear the cloud and the lion.

Thunder and lightning surprised the knight, On the calamitous day in the Najd.’

However, what the narration mentions about the revelation of these verses in the story does not suit the fact that the verses appear to be Meccan, nor does it suit the tone of the verses based on our prior discussions. (13) Also in Al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī cites Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū Shaykh, who narrate from ʿAlī, about the verse, He has guardian angels, to his front and his rear, who guard him by Allah’s

command: ‘There is not a servant except with him are angels, guarding him from a wall collapsing upon him, or falling into a well, or being eaten by a lion, or drowning, or burning. But when the divine determination (al-qadr) comes, they leave him to God’s determination.’

Author’s comment: A narration with the same meaning is narrated from Abū Dāwūd about the divine determination, and Ibn Abī Dunyā, and Ibn ʿAsākir, from him. And a narration with the same meaning is also narrated from Imām al-Bāqir and Imām al-Ṣādiq.

(14) And in Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Fuḍayl b. ʿUthmān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh he mentioned the verse, He has guardian angels (muʿaqqibāt), to his front and his rear, who guard him by Allah’s command. Then he said: ‘From before, from after—the muʿaqqibāt are the righteous deeds that endure (bāqiyāt ṣāliḥāt).’

Author’s comment: The apparent meaning of this tradition is that the righteous deeds that endure are one of the things two which the term muʿaqqibāt used in this verse refers. In other words, these righteous deeds protect their doer from the evil of the divine decree (al-qaḍāʾ), but they do not protect their doer except through the angels who are charged with watching over him. Therefore, the meaning of this tradition accords with what we have presented in our explanation of the verse. And it is possible that ‘from before, from after’ (al-muʾakhkharāt wa al-muqaddamāt) are identical with ‘the righteous deeds that endure,’ and it is clear how this relates to our explanation.

(15) In the same source, it is narrated from Abū ʿAmr al-M adāʾinī from Abū ʿAbd Allāh: ‘Surely, my father used to say: “Indeed, God has made an irrevocable decree that He will not bless a servant with a blessing and then deprive him of it before the servant commits a sin that necessitates the removal of it. This is according to

God’s saying, Indeed Allah does not change a people’s lot, unless they change what is in their souls.”’

(16) And in the same source, it is related from Aḥmad b. Muḥammad, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā, regarding God’s saying, Indeed Allah does not change a people’s lot, unless they change what is in their souls. And when Allah wishes to visit ill on a people, there is nothing that can avert it: ‘So, the matter returns to God, the Exalted.’

Author’s comment: This is a reference to what we have previously explained regarding the meaning of the verse.

(17) And in Maʿānī al-Akhbār, al-Ṣadūq narrates via his chain from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Faḍl, from his father, who said: ‘I heard Abū Khālid al-Kābulī say: “I heard Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn say: ‘The sins that alter blessings are committing wrongs against people and forsaking good habits, making a pretense of virtue, ingratitude for blessings, and abandonment of thanksgiving. God Almighty said, Indeed Allah does not change a people’s lot, unless they change what is in their souls.’”’

(18) And in the same source, via a chain from Ḥasan b. Faḍl, from al-Riḍā, regarding the verse, ) It is He who shows you the lightning, inspiring fear and hope (13:12), He said: ‘Fear of the traveler and hope for the resident.’

(19) And in the Tafsīr al-Nuʿmānī, from al-Aṣbagh b. Nabāta, from ʿAlī regarding God’s saying, though He is great in might (13:13):

‘He means in plotting (makr).’

(20) And in the Āmālī of al-Shaykh al-Ṭūsī, he narrates via his chain from Anas b. Mālik that that the messenger of God sent a man to one of the tyrants of the Arabs, calling him to God Almighty.

He said to the messenger: ‘Inform me about this to which you call me—is it from silver or gold or from iron?’ He returned to the Prophet and informed him of what the ruler had said. The Prophet said: ‘Return to him and invite him.’ He said: ‘O Prophet of God, he is too stubborn for that.’ He said: ‘Return to him.’

The messenger returned and did as he had been told, and while he was speaking to him, a cloud suddenly thundered and cast down a lightning bolt on his head, taking the top of his head of . God Almighty then revealed the verse: ‘…and He releases the thunderbolts and strikes with them whomever He wishes. Yet they dispute

concerning Allah, though He is great in might’ (13:13).

Author’s comment: The same can be said of the end of this story as was said about that of ʿĀmir and Arbad. To this can also be added that there is no basis for this report splitting the revelation verse into different parts, such that only ‘… and He releases the thunderbolts …’ was revealed at this point.

(21) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, it is narrated from Abū al-Jārūd, from from Abī Jaʿfar, regarding the verse, To Allah prostrates whoever there is in the heavens and the earth … (13:15): ‘As for those who prostrate among the inhabitants of the heavens voluntarily, they are the angels, for they prostrate to God voluntarily. As for those who prostrate from the inhabitants of the earth who were born into Islam, they prostrate to Him voluntarily. And as for those who prostrate to Him unwillingly, they are compelled to Islam. And as for those who do not prostrate at all, their shadows prostrate for them in the morning and the evening.’

Author’s comment: The apparent of the narration contradicts the context of the verse under discussion, for the context of the verse is expounding

the fact that He subjugation all beings through His greatness and exaltedness, whether they are in the heavens or the earth, and whether themselves

or even their shadows. The verse informs us of their prostration to Him the Exalted through the essence of prostration. The apparent meaning of the narration is that prostration is used in the literal sense of lowering oneself and placing the forehead on the ground or the like thereof, whether by them or by their shadows. And regardless of whether they actually prostrated willingly or unwillingly or whether the falling of their shadows on

the earth resembles prostration, none of this glorifies God Almighty, contrary to what we have said about the meaning of the verse.

In addition to this, the quoted narration does not accord with the inclusiveness visible in His saying: and their shadows at sunrise and sunset. Clearer than this is the inclusiveness that can be seen in His saying: Have they not regarded that whatever thing Allah has created casts its shadow to the right and to the left, prostrating to Allah in utter humility? To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, including animals and angels, and they are not arrogant (16:48–49).
